abstract: The paper presents an architecture for neural network regulators. The back-propagation algorithm has been used in an integral hierarchical structure to perform I-O mapping and adaptation of controller parameters. This avoids the use of the sign of the plant errors during the back-propagation procedure, and prevents the generation of excessive control signals. It does not require a reference model or inverse system model, or the application of any probing signals. The neural network regulator has a compact structure, which can easily be extended to cater for more complex dynamic systems or additional control loops. The regulator has been evaluated by simulation on a detailed nonlinear model of a turbogenerator system. The results illustrate the good performance which may be achieved with the neural adaptive controller.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Controller design by frequency-weighted approximation-the multivariable case
abstract: The method presented offers an effective and time saving tool for multivariable controller design. The relation between controller complexity and achievable closed-loop system behaviour remains transparent in the design process. In some cases with largely different bandwidths of the diagonal elements of the plant, the described technique tends to achieve the goal of decoupling better than the approximation of the desired transient responses. This is caused by the weighting which in these cases assumes larger values over a broad frequency range for the off-diagonal elements. This can be prevented by the introduction of an additional factor in the weighting to influence the ratio of diagonal to off-diagonal weighting.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Real-time adaptive control using CPAS on a MC68010-based process computer
abstract: Traditionally indirect adaptive controllers are implemented by evaluating the estimation, design and control parts in sequence. This is probably the case more for the sake of convenience than for the nature of the adaptive algorithm, since the estimation and the control parts apart from the design coupling for the 'certainty equivalence principle' based controllers could be independently evaluated. In the paper a multitasking implementation of an indirect adaptive controller is examined. By using the delta -model approximation to a continuous time adaptive controller the benefits of the additional flexibility arising from the multitasking implementation may be easily incorporated in the overall design. The multitasking adaptive controller is implemented through the use of the programming language CPAS and the multitasking operating system SL/OS in this particular case running on a CISC MC68010 process computer.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Evaluation of fault tolerant software structures for parallel systems in industrial control
abstract: Computing systems are being used increasingly in applications which demand safe and reliable operation at all times. However, fault-free operation under all operational circumstances cannot be guaranteed. Fault tolerance is achieved by including in the system design special mechanisms which recognise and override automatically the effects of the fault, giving a satisfactory performance even in the presence of the fault. In the paper these software fault tolerant structures are applied to a real-time robotics application distributed over a number of transputers. The design and implementation language is Occam. The effectiveness of these structures against faults is measured both in terms of data integrity and performance aspects. The paper shows the effectiveness of certain software fault tolerance mechanisms when applied to a parallel system, with real time responses.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Discontinuous controller for robot tracking control
abstract: A control principle suitable for a robot positioning mechanism is proposed. The basic idea of the control law is to make use of the favorable properties of time optimal and linear controllers. A time optimal controller is used in the range of high deviations with respect to the reference position value by considering the constrained control signal. In this mode of operation only the maximal dynamics is required. In the range of low deviations with respect to the position error signal, the linear servocontroller is activated and the remaining error is eliminated. Due to low signal levels there is no danger that the actuators will exceed the constraint.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Vibration testing control using spectral warping
abstract: Concerns the generation and analysis of random processes in automatic vibration testing systems. Discrete Fourier transforms (DFT) are used. The digital signal processing technique of spectral warping offers the possibility of increasing the effectiveness of the DFT used in implementing such tasks. This technique consists of transforming the original sequence to a new one having the property that equally-spaced frequency samples of its DFT are identical to unequally-spaced frequency samples of the DFT of the original sequence. This opens up the possibility of decreasing the array size of the DFT and thereby increasing its performance, as measured, for example, by its speed of execution. A general organisational structure and a functional algorithm are proposed for a vibration testing control system, which makes use of this spectral warping approach.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Weighting function specification in H/sub infinity / design (military helicopter)
abstract: This paper describes the application of H/sub infinity / to the design of a controller for a battlefield helicopter. It shows the effect of the choice of the weighting functions on the performance of the resulting closed loop system, and given some indication of how to utilise the freedom of choice. The appropriate handling qualities requirements documents describe the response shapes that are desirable for particular flight conditions, and these should be used as guidelines for further development of the cost function weights. Bandwidths on selected channels can be manipulated to a certain extent by moving the sensitivity function weights, and overshoots can be corrected by careful targeting of the rate feedback channel weights. Actuator movements can be monitored by examining time responses, and these give useful indicators of the feasibility of any design changes.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Application of a distributed generalised predictive controller for adaptive control of a crystal growth process
abstract: Describes a distributed generalized predictive controller (DGPC) which has been successfully applied to a crystal growth process based on the temperature oscillation method. The proper selection of the sampling period for every loop is made by a supervisor module. Good quality control has been achieved in the two possible modes of operation-periodically oscillating source temperature and periodically oscillating crystal temperature. Long term adaptive control shows stability and high performance of the DGPC during the whole experiment.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Identification of the pure time delay of a process
abstract: Previous work by the author has produced a novel scheme for controlling processes with pure time delay, Mitchell (1987, 1990). This scheme uses a model of the minimum phase elements of the process to generate the necessary control signals. This model must provide an accurate representation of the process, and so must be adaptive and identified continually. The identification method used is the recursive least squares algorithm and this produces a suitable model. However, the method requires that the value of the time delay of the process be known. Usually this is assumed as a priori information, but even if its value is known, it may change during the operation of the process. In the paper various methods are considered for identifying the time delay, and then a new method developed by the author is described and its performance evaluated.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Parallel algorithms for the implementation of linear repetitive systems stability tests
abstract: The paper considers the computations associated with stability analysis for linear repetitive systems and, in particular, the so-called differential unit memory sub-class which are of direct industrial relevance. The results presented consist of basic algorithms for hypercube based parallel computation of a frequency response matrix which is, in effect, the basis of one set of stability tests for this case. Further, some possible areas for further development of these highly promising initial results are briefly discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Guaranteed H/sub infinity / Disturbance attenuation and l/sub 1/ control and output bounds with LEB regulators
abstract: Most of the standard regulator solutions applicable to linear systems focus only on time-domain or frequency-domain results. Some techniques accommodate mixed-domain performance specifications providing solutions through the use of numerical optimization but do not give insight on the conditions under which such solutions exist or how to perform tradeoffs. The article presents a technique by which it is possible to find a regulator to make a linear system satisfy control and output l/sub 1/-norm bounds and, modifying them, to achieve a desired H/sub infinity /-norm of the disturbance-to-output transfer function. A linear-ellipsoidal-bounded formulation is involved. Also, frequency weightings are added to the input and states of the original plant to allow more flexibility in the frequency domain.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Fine-tuned QFT control in a Matlab environment
abstract: Quantitative feedback theory (QFT) is used to design a robust controller which reduces the loop sensitivity to parameter variations for a desired response. To ameliorate the trade-off between sensitivity and sensor noise amplification highlighted by Gawthrop (1988) the robust controller is used as a coarse controller and self-tuning is used for fine tuning around the loop. The paper also investigates the quality of control through computer simulation. The design procedure adopted in Horowitz and Sidi (1972) and Farsi et al. (1989) is very complex, so, a computer package PC-Matlab, has been developed to ease the various steps.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Pressure control within an industrial plasticating extruder
abstract: Describes the design of a control strategy for an extruder gearpump arrangement which yields substantial improvement in operation. The controller design is based on the discrete optimal regulator solution and includes automatic dead-time compensation. The selection of an appropriate sampling time is obviously important in any discrete time design and the paper presents the results of an algorithm for automatic selection of the most appropriate sampling time. To provide realistic comparison of the performance of this strategy with the existing PI feedforward implementation a simple extension to a optimal regulation strategy which includes feedforward action is presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Industrial applications of advanced multivariable control
abstract: Describes work in progress on the following two projects: intelligent robot control using an integrated H/sup infinity //adaptive controller in a two degrees-of-freedom configuration; and the application of H/sup infinity / optimal control to the design of a wide-envelope full authority active control system for a generic high performance single main rotor helicopter. Both projects are in the early stages of development but the results so far are encouraging with the advanced multivariable control methods used pointing to significant benefits over more conventional techniques. The authors demonstrate the power and flexibility of MATLAB as well as illustrating the potential of H/sup infinity / techniques.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Modified two-step approach to the solution of constrained nonlinear optimisation problems
abstract: The basic idea of the modified two-step approach in optimising control is adopted to design an algorithm for the solution of constrained nonlinear optimisation problems. The algorithm is less sensitive to the Hessian structure of the problem than many existing optimisation algorithms and, hence, more effective for solving ill-conditioned problems. Optimality and convergence analyses are provided. Practical issues concerning algorithm implementation, such as model based optimisation, model matrix and iterative gain selection, are discussed and computer simulations show that the algorithm is very efficient.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A fuzzy logic based method for the synthesis of controllers for nonlinear systems
abstract: The paper shows how off-line methods can be used where an analytical description of the system is available, such that real-time control can be achieved using very simple general purpose processors, or very fast application specific integrated circuits (ASIC's). The method of table lookup based on fuzzy system states derived from the system characteristics has been shown to be feasible, and control of the balancing rod achieved.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The application of self-tuning control strategies to the active reduction of sound
abstract: The generalised minimum variance (GMV) strategy is proposed for the active reduction of sound, and it is shown that, under certain constraints, the more usual adaptive filtering control strategy is a special control law of the GMV strategy. Using both theoretical derivations and simulation experiments it is shown that the GMV strategy is a valuable extension of the usual strategies. Adaptive filtering appears to be suitable for a restricted class of disturbance signals. If the disturbance signal consists of a measurable part and a Gaussian noise part, the performance of the adaptive filtering controller is very good. The rate of convergence may be slow, as the acoustic process poles can be poorly damped. If the stochastic noise contribution to the disturbance signal is non-Gaussian, however, the performance of the adaptive filtering system seriously deteriorates. In that case feedback control should be applied. The GMV strategy is capable of reducing a measurable disturbance by feedforward control and a stochastic disturbance by feedback control. In general, the GMV control with both feedforward and feedback yields a much better performance than a pure feedback or an adaptive filtering strategy. A complication with the GMV control strategy, however, is to find an appropriate choice for the weighting polynomials in the cost function, when the secondary acoustic process is nonminimum phase. If necessary, these polynomials can also be used to place the closed-loop poles at well-damped positions.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The robotic assembly of underwear
abstract: Describes the problem of robotic based fabric handling as seen by the Robotics Research Unit at Hull University. The third phase of this project, following success in ply separation and robotic sewing, is to produce a prototype robotic assembly line for a complete garment. The line is designed for assembling mens' Y-fronts and ladies' briefs. The project is subdivided into two dimensional component based assembly, three dimensional folding and closing operations, and a supervisory computer system to aid communication and reconfiguration. The manual operations for constructing these garments are mentioned in this paper, outlining the handling difficulties and the required system goals in terms of cost and performances. The various robotic handling solutions are described in detail, together with an assessment of their performance. Conclusions include the implications of the techniques used in this assembly line on solving the problems associated with products of a similar nature.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Performance of model-reference adaptive control algorithms under non-ideal conditions
abstract: The design of an adaptive control system is normally based on the assumption that the plant to be controlled belongs to a class with a given structure, only the parameter values being unknown. Typical assumptions are that the plant is linear, time-invariant and stably invertible, with a known time-delay and an upper bound on the dynamical order. In order to gain some insight into this question, the author considers a type of discrete-time model-reference adaptive control scheme, which can readily be modified so as to improve its robustness. First, the author describes the basic structure and presents some general results concerning its stability and convergence properties. The author then investigates some simple special cases, with the aim of being able to draw tentative conclusions about what may be expected to happen in situations too complicated for detailed analysis.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Robust, low norm multirate control using eigenstructure assignment
abstract: Examines the application of an eigenstructure assignment optimisation technique which makes full use of the robustness properties offered by a class of multivariable, multirate systems, namely multiple-input, fixed-output (MIFO) sample rate systems. Two multirate design examples, based on the control of an aircraft lateral subsystem using state feedback, illustrate the application of this method.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Stabilization of nonlinearly coupled uncertain systems
abstract: Concerns uncertain systems with global asymptotic stability of the zero state. It is assumed that the structure of the uncertain systems can be modelled as two nonlinearly coupled subsystems, together with uncertainty in each of the subsystems. For each uncertain system, a class of discontinuous feedback controls is presented which renders the system zero state globally asymptotically stable. The feedback stabilization problem consists of two stages. In the first, a nonlinear manifold W, containing the state origin, is constructed with the property that, if it is rendered invariant by suitable feedback, then all solutions in W tend to the state origin. In the second, a feedback control is designed which renders W both invariant and globally finite-time attractive, and the zero state of the differential inclusion system globally attractive. This manifold may be interpreted as a global centre manifold.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A non-minimum state space approach to true digital control based on delta -operator models
abstract: Previous publications have introduced the concept of 'true digital control' (TDC) and discussed a novel non-minimum state space (NMSS) approach to the identification, estimation and true digital control of dynamic systems described by transfer function models in the backward shift (z/sup -1/) operator. In this paper, the authors show how the same NMSS approach can be applied to systems described by the alternative but related delta ( delta ) operator transfer function model and introduces the conditions for the controllability of the model. The state variable feedback control law associated with this NMSS model can be defined either for closed loop pole assignment (PA) or optimal linear quadratic control. The former PA control algorithm is developed and applied to a simple second order process. Recursive instrumental variable (IV) procedures for the identification and estimation of delta -operator models are then described and shown to be optimal and sub-optimal generalisations of methods proposed previously for continuous-time systems. Finally, the paper re-visits the simple second order model and presents illustrative simulation results which demonstrate the efficacy of the complete TDC design procedure.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Performance characteristics of adaptive gain feedback
abstract: Considers some of the performance characteristics of adaptive gain feedback (AGF) systems. Using an example it is shown analytically that AGF improves the matching of the plant to the reference model. A right half plane zero approximation of the plant transfer function is derived using the singular perturbation model developed by Ioannou and Kokotovic (1983). From this analysis a value for the adaptive gain parameter is established. The analysis then involves using an approach developed by Astrom (1983) to investigate the frequency dependence of the adaptive parameters. The affect of tuning the AGF parameter is demonstrated by means of simulation results which shows the beneficial effects of AGF.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Predictive functional control of flexible structures: a composite control approach
abstract: A composite control of flexible structures is designed according to a multirate time strategy. The main control concerns the slow dynamics while fast control damps the high frequency modes. Both controllers are designed by using the predictive functional control technique. The frequency separation hypothesis on which the control design is based, turns out to be less restrictive for applications. Performance and robustness properties of the proposed design are illustrated through simulation results. The strategy appears to be very robust against parameter variations.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Smoother sliding mode controller for SCSM-based position servo system
abstract: A smooth sliding mode controller is designed for a position servo system based on a self-controlled synchronous motor. Using this controller, it is possible for the phase plane trajectory to move smoothly along the sliding line, even with a lower switching frequency. To ensure that the controller is used effectively in a disturbed environment, a simple parameter estimation method is also proposed. The effectiveness of both the sliding mode controller and the parameter estimation method is demonstrated by computer simulations. As the demanded control activity (the DC link current) is decreased, a large amount of energy can be saved; and as the switching frequency can be reduced without surpassing the accepted overshoot of the system, the switching devices will last long. The sliding mode controller proposed is not only effective, but also simple in controller structures and intuitive in controller parameter design.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Design of multilevel pseudorandom signals for specified harmonic content
abstract: Pseudorandom signals have been used as test signals in system identification for many years. The most common application is the identification of linear systems using pseudorandom binary signals, which have excellent correlation properties for this purpose. In contrast, the harmonic properties of pseudorandom signals are less well known than their correlation properties. Consequently the harmonic properties of these signals have been less well exploited in system identification. In the paper, the harmonic properties of pseudorandom signals are shown to depend on fundamental properties of the maximum-length m-sequences from which they are derived by mapping, and on the nature of the mapping itself. In particular, it is shown that both the m-sequence and the mapping can be chosen to provide the pseudorandom signal with a specified harmonic content.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Review of hybrid and continuous-time self-tuning controllers and analysis of an LQ design
abstract: A review of various explicit self-tuning control schemes is presented and both the parameter estimation and control law are discussed. A hybrid indirect, linear quadratic (LQ), self-tuning control of a continuous-time linear plant is investigated. In this paper, the 'hybrid' algorithm implements the parameter estimation and controller parameter adjustment on a discrete-time basis and the control loop operates in continuous-time. Comparisons are given of continuous-time, hybrid and discrete-time LQ self-tuning controllers for the simulation of a DC motor position controlled servo-system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: World modelling from range images
abstract: The author separates data fusion, a process central to creating world models, into two phases: interpretation and update. A standard technique from model based vision, the interpretation tree, is applied to the first phase. General methods of controlling the search space are reviewed and a framework for incorporating such methods suggested. Particular methods for the case of a laser range finder in an indoors environment are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Networked control systems-plant interfacing issues
abstract: The paper looks at the problems associated with designing LANs that incorporate direct ('passive node') interfacing to controlling elements. Two general schemes based on the token-bus principle suitable for use in such fast real-time applications are described. Their performances are evaluated (using simulation studies) in terms of system responsiveness and fault tolerance within the context of distributed real-time systems. It is finally highlighted that no single scheme provides a global networking solution for distributed control applications. As a result, in the design of high speed real-time LANs, the organisation of passive nodes is largely dictated by the nature of specific application requirements.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Nonperiodic binary signals with good autocorrelation properties
abstract: A survey of the available types of nonperiodic binary signals with near-impulsive nonperiodic autocorrelation functions, for application in identification. It is shown that some of these are suitable for linear system identification applications. In the case of complementary signals, it is also possible to synthesise a theoretically unlimited number of uncorrelated sets which can be employed for multi-input system identification. Other applications for such sequences include communication channel sounding and data transmission system synchronisation, and it is mainly for these purposes that they have been applied.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Investigation of a light, redundant manipulator for in-orbit applications
abstract: The concept of a light, redundant manipulator for in-orbit applications is presented, along with a brief investigation of two control schemes. The configuration control method is analysed by simulating its control effectiveness on a 4-link dynamic model, using ACSL and Pro-Matlab. The results of the simulation show the feasibility of using the configuration control method though the definition of suitable kinematic functions for the addition tasks can introduce difficulties. Problems, such as extra algorithmic singularities and conflicts between the primary and secondary tasks, may result if inappropriate kinematic functions are selected.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Tandem control of a gas pressure reduction station
abstract: In general, a typical pressure reduction control system is configured as two parallel flow streams each containing two pressure regulators connected in series. The main controlling elements used for the analysis presented in the paper are IGA axial flow regulators and the installations are usually referred to as pressure reduction stations (PRS's). Initial investigations revealed the need for a better understanding of the operation and limitations of this particular regulator since, in certain circumstances, its behaviour was unpredictable. It was therefore decided that a mathematical model would be derived which emulated the regulator under all operational conditions, which would then enable the development of an appropriate microprocessor control system. Following this, a complete system specification could be derived leading to physical implementation. The paper presents the initial development of the model for the axial flow regulator, together with results obtained from a preliminary validation exercise. In addition, the paper describes the development of a control system which will enable tandem operation throughout the PRS's operational envelope.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Sophisticated motion control systems with a high-level computer language
abstract: Motion control covers a very wide spectrum of options. There is the choice between DC, AC, or stepper motors, open or closed loop control and a range of various digital motion controllers to suit. Building these components into a high-speed multi-motion system is not so easily achieved, especially with a clearly defined strategy for future expansion and compatibility with existing and planned computer, PLC and networking systems. The choice of hardware and software options for quickly building motion control systems is discussed emphasising the need to encompass many parameters in addition to those of motion to solve the actual machine requirements, together with the increasing need for diagnostics both local and remote as the control systems become more complex.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Control strategies in the active isolation of engineering systems
abstract: Active and semi-active vibration isolation methods are applied to many engineering systems. Typical applications are to rotorcraft vibration isolation systems and vehicle suspension. In this study both rotor vibration and vehicle suspensions are dealt with. Control strategies are studied in a simulated form by providing the characteristics of a controller via software. The approach described in providing control strategies is to use the multivariable state feedback control techniques to reduce the vibration level applied to the mechanical structure. Specifically the pole placement method is used to guarantee the stability of the rotor isolation system and at the same time to achieve sufficient gain and phase margins of the dominant closed-loop poles. Based on a frequency domain method, disturbance zeros are created which can eventually lead to complete elimination of the vibration level applied to a helicopter structure.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A behaviour classification for integrated process supervision
abstract: The paper proposes a classification of system behaviours that allows the generic control methods to be identified and clearly related. It then presents a strategy for integrated process supervision that provides for controlled evolution through the different control regimes. The generality of the strategy is independent of a particular realisation of individual control regimes, thereby allowing AI methods and classical control techniques to co-exist within an integrated framework. The system has been fully implemented on a SUN 3/160 workstation and validated on a laboratory scale process rig. An overview of the results obtained from a scheme utilising a standard three-term controller, a simple adaptive system and fault diagnosis based on a qualitative model of the process rig is presented. The paper then presents the behaviour classification for continuous processes. These are then related to a set of generic control regimes i.e. primary control, adaptive control and fault diagnosis. The structure of the integrated process supervision scheme is given, and its realisation for the control of the process rig is briefly described. Experimental results are given. Remarks on the effectiveness of the scheme and its future extensions are presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Diagnosing continuous dynamic systems using qualitative simulation
abstract: Concerns model-based diagnosis of dynamic systems (MBDDS) by fuzzy qualitative simulation (FUSIM). Within a primitive architecture, the system model explicitly describes the structure of the plant to be diagnosed and an algorithm for generating the dynamic behaviour from the plant's structure. The discrepancy generator compares observations from the plant with predictions from the system model and generates appropriate discrepancies, whilst the candidate generator uses the discrepancies to produce candidates, i.e., the possible faults, to be validated by the system model. The diagnostic supervisor contains the meta-knowledge necessary to control the diagnostic process. This paper discusses how this diagnostic method determines the fault conditions of a physical system. The FUSIM algorithm produces a sequence of system states with related temporal durations, providing a significant advantage over other qualitative simulation techniques for refining diagnosis over time. An implementation of the primitive architecture is described. The mechanism for the comparison between the predictions and the observations is presented; it is the key technique for system-monitoring and fault evaluation, and the basis for discrepancy generation within MBDDS.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Parametric uncertainty modelling and real and complex structured singular value computation applied to an electro-mechanical system
abstract: The investigation of closed-loop systems subject to model perturbations is an important issue in order to assume stability robustness of a control design. A large variety of model perturbations can be described by norm-bounded uncertainty models. In this paper a general approach for modelling structured complex and real-valued parametric perturbations is presented. The resulting robustness analysis problem is solved nonconservatively using real and complex structured singular value calculations. The uncertainty modelling and the robustness analysis are shown for a high-accuracy 5D electromechanical positioning device to be used in optical recording.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A functional programming environment for CACSD and data management
abstract: An engineering design environment should allow users to design complex engineering systems, to manage and coordinate the designs as they proceed, and to develop and modify the software tools used for designs. These requirements call for a programming environment with an integrated set of software tools of different functionalities. The required functionalities are mainly: the provision of design algorithms based on suitable numeric software, appropriate data structures for the application area, the provision of a design database for the long term management of the designs generated and a user-friendly interface. The provision of such an integrated design environment in a functional programming language environment with particular emphasis on the provision of appropriate control-theoretic data structures and a semantic database is described. A functional data model forms the basis of the database model. Structural properties, and relationships are modelled as functions mapping entities to values or other entities. Entities are classified entity types with inheritance semantics.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Use of the coherence function for a comparison of test signals for frequency domain identification
abstract: The coherence function has proved useful for aiding in the design of a frequency domain identification experiment. For consistent and reliable estimation of system parameters, making use of frequency domain identification techniques the main requirement is that the coherence function be close to unity and have a flat characteristic over a sufficiently wide bandwidth. For efficient estimation the input test signal length and peak factor, along with the type of signal which is best suited to the experiment are also important factors. The paper provides a comparison of these and other properties of commonly used test signals such as linear and logarithmic swept sinewaves, binary m-sequences and multi-harmonic test signals.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Fast integrated system optimization and parameter estimation algorithms
abstract: It is proposed to use a gradient approximation in efficient second order nonlinear programming algorithms like conjugate gradient and variable metric techniques to obtain the second order ISOPE algorithms. Three alternative approaches based on this idea are investigated and verified through numerical simulation. Suitable line search algorithms are designed in order to appreciate the quality of the gradient approximation at a given iteration. Sufficient general purpose conditions for the algorithms convergence are derived and discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Modelling and identification of electrode position controller in electric arc furnace
abstract: Electrode position controller in electric arc furnace systems plays an important role in the steel-making process by which a reference arc impedance or arc current is maintained to guarantee steady power input to the steel in the furnace. Modelling and identification of the electrode position controller is a prerequisite for realization of its direct digital control. In this paper, detailed physical analysis of the arc characteristic in electric arc furnace is given, and a model of electric arc furnace electrode controller for one phase is proposed. An identification strategy is then presented to deal with the model's identification problem.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Adaptive force control of a two-actuator system in dynamic structural testing
abstract: A model of a two-actuator system operating on a cantilever beam is presented. Results obtained from simulations of single and two-actuator systems operating on the beam confirm that a pole-placement self-tuner is adequate for controlling the applied forces in accordance with prescribed patterns even when the flow gain varies significantly and other nonlinearities are included. Application of the self-tuner to a nonlinear high order model is presented and discussed. It is found that the estimator may fail due to the low frequency of the demand signal but this failure can be avoided by using a variable forgetting factor or by resetting the covariance matrix. In the multivariable case, the results obtained demonstrate the feasibility of controlling a strongly coupled two-actuator system. It is found that by appropriate selection of the desired closed-loop polynomial matrix such that it contains a faster pole for the loop associated with the actuator closer to the root of the cantilever, the interaction effect can be reduced considerably.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A design study on the control of warship rolling motion using rudder and stabilising fins
abstract: Presents the results of a design study into the feasibility of improving warship roll stabilisation using an integrated rudder and stabilising fin control strategy. The primary advantage of the proposed control strategy is that rudder roll stabilisation and enhanced roll stabilisation can be achieved using existing sensors and actuators, and requires only minimal additional hardware and expenditure to implement. In addition, the proposed control strategy provides the Command with the flexibility to select the mode by which roll stabilisation is achieved. A decision which can be made in the light of the tactical situation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Model-based expert system for computer aided design of feedback controllers
abstract: Describes the development of an expert system environment for control design using an expert system shell interfaced with MATLAB. Reasoning is based upon the use of approximate plant models and robust control methods are interpreted as procedures for rule validation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Reconfigurable flight control systems
abstract: This paper concerns a proposed reconfiguration control scheme for application with a generic fighter aircraft which has eight control surfaces, and whose longitudinal and lateral motions are to be controlled simultaneously. The mathematical model of the aircraft dynamics is presented first, and is followed by a brief description of the aircraft's closed loop response, obtained using a baseline automatic flight control system (AFCS). The effects upon the dynamic performance of this baseline AFCS of sensor, controller, actuator, and control surface failures, of several different types, are illustrated and discussed, before the effectiveness of an analytical redundancy scheme in countering controller or sensor failures is demonstrated. Some other reconfiguration schemes are briefly discussed, then yet another method, used by the authors, is presented in relation to its effectiveness in achieving the objectives of the reconfiguration.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Multivariable controller design for industrial repetitive processes
abstract: Considers controller design for industrial repetitive processes. In particular, the concept of a memoryless dynamic unity negative feedback control scheme is introduced for a sub-class of direct industrial relevance. A systematic procedure for designing this scheme to solve the so-called limit profile design problem is developed based, in effect, on simulation-based stability tests. The application of this procedure to one special case is detailed to demonstrate its basic feasibility and highlight some possible future research areas.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A new technique for fault detection in multi-sensor probes
abstract: Proposes a novel approach to determine the self consistency of the observed values from a collection of sensors. While the original techniques were developed for deterministic chaotic systems, the generalizations presented apply to both deterministic and stochastic systems. The authors deal with the case where a particular process or system is observed by a large number of sensors, each measuring some distinct characteristic of the system. In brief, the approach distinguishes observations which correspond to physically realizable states from those which represent physically nonrealizable states; the latter implying error in the observation (i.e. sensor error).<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: SIMULAB an integrated environment for simulation and control
abstract: Command-driven matrix languages, such as MATLAB, have proved successful for linear control system design. The paper discusses the development and integration of SIMULAB, a graphically oriented nonlinear simulation package, into MATLAB. The 'open system' philosophy of MATLAB is carried over into SIMULAB where blocks and analysis tools can be added to the package. With access to MATLAB's powerful command language new algorithms for simulation, linearization and trimming have been developed. A system calling syntax, known as an S-function, is used to characterize SIMULAB systems. S-functions, which can be coded in a variety of ways, including block diagrams, C, FORTRAN, or M-files, provide a means for the incorporation of SIMULAB systems into the MATLAB command set. The complete design cycle involving modelling, simulation, and control design is addressed with respect to SIMULAB's simulation tools and MATLAB's toolboxes for system identification, control design, and optimization.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The manipulation of 3D fabric shapes
abstract: Outlines a project which addresses the problems of linking simple manipulation cells together in order to achieve automatic garment manufacture. A prototype assembly line is under development at Hull in which a series of autonomous, adaptable robot cells are linked together to assemble two different garment types. Several kinds of knitted cottons have been assessed with this assembly line and all of the 2D structures have been successfully assembled automatically. Work began to automate the final three seams and these are illustrated in figure 2. These seams involve two 3D/2D operations and one 3D/3D operation. A gripper was designed which automates the construction of the last three seams and is described in the paper.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Explicit adaptive control of nonminimum phase systems with a class of preload nonlinearities
abstract: An adaptive control scheme extended from the linear method given by Chai (1990) and Hersh and Zarrop (1986) is developed to deal with a nonlinear system, which has the same nonlinearity as described by Kung and Womack (1984), but the linear part can be nonminimum phase system and the assumption for b/sub 0/ is not necessary in the design. Besides, by using the design method, the desired characteristics of the closed-loop system can be prespecified. Under suitable conditions, the algorithm will ensure that the closed-loop system is stable and convergent with a specific residue.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An adaptive control model for parallel program scheduling
abstract: Explores the role of learning techniques motivated by the approaches in artificial intelligence in the context of improving parallel program performance. The authors present an adaptive control model to improve the parallel program performance through dynamic modification of scheduling parameters under various run-time environments. Optimal or improved scheduling strategies learned from previous program executions provide feedback to further program executions.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Design of adaptive digital PID controllers incorporating linear quadratic compensators
abstract: The problem of loss of co-primeness in recursively identified ARMA models is discussed, and its impact on a large class of multivariable pole-assignment controllers is elucidated. On this basis, an adaptive digital controller is proposed based on a multivariable PID controller incorporating an inner-loop linear quadratic compensator. This control-law circumvents the problems which can be experienced, due to loss of co-primeness of the identified ARMA model, using the adaptive PID controller incorporating inner-loop pole-assignment as proposed by B. Porter and C.L. Body (1989). The effectiveness of such an adaptive digital controller is illustrated by designing an adaptive set-point tracking controller for the F-16 aircraft in a flight condition for which this aircraft is open-loop unstable.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Boiler soot-blowing optimisation for power generation plant
abstract: Although the potential financial rewards accruing from the development of effective soot-blowing for large coal-fired boilers is well known, closed-loop control of soot-blowers has received little, if any, attention. For this reason, this paper which describes ongoing research in the area, first gives an overview of the subject. The paper then describes modifications, necessary to the basic heat transfer models used to determine boiler cleanliness. This modified on-line heat transfer model, which is demonstrated to be superior to the normal basic models, is then combined with an expert system. Closed-loop control may then be achieved, by using the output from the expert system to drive sequential soot-blowers.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Developing a learning system capable of hypothesis justification (fault diagnosis)
abstract: Learning systems of all kinds are being investigated for potential uses in a wide variety of applications. These systems have a peculiar strength, that of abstracting a solution to a problem, increasing enormously the size of the domain of problems considerably. The wide variety of learning systems under investigation and development have individual benefits associated with their respective architectures, few however have a structure that permits an investigation into their processing by people other than their developers. Often the ability to offer some form of justification is a highly desirable feature. The paper offers some of the strong points of learning systems in general and proposes a learning system architecture with the ability to justify clearly the steps used to reach a result, in an industrial application. The application considered is fault diagnosis of a power network.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A controller design method for large-scale systems in the frequency domain
abstract: A novel frequency-domain controller design method for multivariable, large-scale systems is introduced. The method consists of four distinct phases and systematic techniques for the completion of each phase of the design process are used.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Real-time adaptive control of electrical power and enthalpy for a 750 MW once-through boiler
abstract: The authors investigate a power station represented by a 765 MW combinational block, consisting of a generator/steam turbine unit providing 652.5 MW an another unit providing 112.5 MW. The coal-fired once-through boiler is looked at. The conventional control scheme and a modified adaptive model reference control strategy are compared.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Meeting the demands of batch control
abstract: A major growth area in process control applications is that of 'Speciality' chemicals. The specific industrial sectors involved are pharmaceuticals, organic chemicals, agro-chemicals, and polymers, where an abundance of high value added products are being manufactured. These require complex and numerous process stages carried out in multi-purpose vessels on plant specifically designed for multi-product batch manufacture.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Coordination of economy and quality in power system generation control
abstract: A novel and efficient algorithm has been proposed for automatic generation control by coordination of economic dispatching control (EDC) and load frequency control. The dynamic economic dispatching control for determining the reference output of each generator in each time period is described. In the event small variations should arise in the assumed load, the load frequency control for maintaining the demand-supply balance and for holding the frequency at the prescribed level is discussed. The effectiveness and validity of the proposed coordination algorithm are demonstrated by numerical examples over a model system. Furthermore, problems to be solved for implementation in real time systems are also summarized.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A switched H/sub infinity / strategy for control of a submarine
abstract: Discusses the application of H/sub infinity / optimisation techniques to the design of a control system for a submarine. The dynamics of a submarine change significantly with speed, and to cover the speed envelope from 3 to 18 knots the authors have developed a strategy based on switching of H/sub infinity / controllers. The necessary compensation to achieve bumpless transfer during switching is also the basis of a controller conditioning strategy for maintaining performance in the presence of actuator saturations. Nonlinear simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach. These implementation issues are crucial if multivariable controllers are to find widespread application is industrial (nonlinear) applications.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Early detection of steam leaks in nuclear plant
abstract: As emergency scenarios arise it is essential that the operator of a nuclear power station is not overloaded with irrelevant information. Thus the need for informative monitoring systems as an integral part of the nuclear plant are necessary to ensure the workload of the operator is not unduly increased, especially during high stress situations. A fuzzy safety monitoring system for the early detection of steam links in Royal Navy nuclear steam raising plant is described. The system is based on an interpretation into a set of fuzzy rules of the internal representation of a supervisor employed in monitoring given plant parameters.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Convergence of a multi-input adaptive extremum controller
abstract: The paper describes a self-tuning model-based approach to extremum control where a number of control variables can be manipulated in order to maximize a scalar output. A number of possible estimation models are considered and the local convergence properties of the resulting self-tuning algorithms are investigated.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: ProDynSA-a package of tools for linear dynamic systems analysis written in Prolog
abstract: Support for the computer-aided analysis of dynamic systems has traditionally been provided by numerical tools often written in Fortran. This has often meant that the problem to be analysed must firstly be re-formulated into a matrix representation with which the numerical tools can work. This places a significant load on the user and may be one reason why dynamic systems analysis tools have been slow to find widespread use. The authors describe a prototype, interactive systems definition and analysis package based on block diagrams, called ProDynSA. This package provides a selection of tools for system manipulation and symbolic algebra and can be used as a pre-processing system for numerical analysis packages as well as a powerful analysis system in its own right.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The development of expert systems for process monitoring in BNFL
abstract: British Nuclear Fuels plc (BNFL) is one of only two companies in the world that is able to offer nuclear fuel manufacture, enrichment, reprocessing and waste management services. BNFL has become involved in the development of expert systems for the monitoring of process plants at Sellafield, Springfields and Capenhurst. The author describes the development work which has been undertaken to date and the role of the installed systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A singular value decomposition approach to multivariable GPC
abstract: In the paper the authors look at characteristic decomposition and multivariable generalised predictive control (GPC), singular value decomposition, and time domain computation of the principal direction sequences. All the results of the paper are brought together in the development of a suitable multivariable GPC algorithm which is tested by means of a suitable design study. Comparisons with an earlier algorithm (Kouvaritakis and Rossiter, 1989) are drawn.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Modelling and control of automotive suspension systems
abstract: This paper considers the methodology for simulation and control of automotive suspension systems. The study is motivated by the need for modelling techniques that allow both nonlinear simulations of handling manoeuvres and suspension control studies. The first model developed represents one corner of a vehicle and consists of a sprung mass, unsprung mass and the major suspension links to allow the suspension geometry effects to be incorporated. This vehicle chassis model was built using the multibody system modelling package SD/FAST and the continuous simulation language ACSL. The resultant model was then used to address the ride control problem, using a variety of control techniques. All control design and analysis was undertaken using the scientific and engineering software package, MATLAB.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Feedback stabilization of nonlinear time lag systems
abstract: A simple memoryless state feedback control law is derived for a class of nonlinear time lag systems. Some well known techniques are used to transform a nonlinear time lag system in suitable coordinates in which the design of the control law is straightforward. In certain cases, the asymptotic stability of the closed loop system is ensured independently of delay values.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Software tools for small scale process controllers using a real-time rule interpreter and object-oriented techniques
abstract: Numerous CASE tools are available for large systems, but many relatively simple applications employing embedded microprocessors do not need these large costly tools, which anyway have to be used by specialists. There is a lack of low cost CASE tools suitable for small projects. In many of these cases, products must be tailored to individual customers needs; smaller firms frequently specialise in these areas, yet such firms are just those who are unlikely to employ specialist software engineers. The person with the best knowledge of the customer's real requirements is the sales or applications engineer; they are therefore the person best able to produce the applications software. Inevitably such a non-specialist needs considerable help from the CASE system. The paper describes work in an advanced stage of development which seeks to answer this problem; ways in which control strategies can be implemented correctly are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Identification of synchronous machine models using power spectral analysis
abstract: The authors implement the spectral analysis approach on digital computers for the identification of two generator models; namely, the on-line and off-line models, and describe the conditions of the various tests to be performed for the identification purpose. Furthermore, the authors present an experimental set-up to perform the identification of the off-line model.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Robotic tactile sensing using dynamic techniques
abstract: Shows how dynamic sensing, using very simple sensors, can give details on the nature of an object that at present can only be found using complex and expensive systems. The author studies the relative sensing abilities of robotic sensors, ranging from simple, but robust and reliable micro-switches, to the advanced tactile arrays. These sensors are then analyzed in terms of their data gathering capacity, and using this information it is possible to make a comparison of the capabilities of 'static' and 'dynamic' sensing systems. Based on these predictions the performance of a 'dynamic' sensor is tested and analyzed, and it is shown that outputs from this system are of a high enough standard that object textures can be easily differentiated providing in addition a rudimentary object recognition ability.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Robust adaptive motion control of rigid robots subject to input and output bounded disturbances
abstract: Addresses the problem of controlling rigid robots subject to joints velocity measurements and torque input bounded disturbances. The new control law is based on the algorithms studied in Slotine and Li (1988) and Sadegh and Horowitz (1987), with an e/sub 1/-modification in the parameters update law. A priori knowledge on the bounds of the plant parameters and disturbance is not required but it is shown that it can be used to improve the control performance. The system input and output are shown to be bounded in both cases.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Auto-tuning of a LQ controller for industrial motion control
abstract: Proposes a motion control autotuner for handling systems driven by electrical servomotors. The latter is characterized by its ease of use and high performances: fast tracking dynamics without overshoot, offset-free positioning, and appropriate stability margin. The specifications have been defined from the conclusions of a survey of heavy motion control users such as car manufacturers and mechanical constructors. A real-time experimental evaluation is given to show the performances of the autotuner. The involved autotuning experiments are consistent with a safe operating mode of the mechanical systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Optimal filtering and Kalman filtering using MATLAB
abstract: The aim of this paper is to illustrate the ease with which data recorded from a complex nonlinear system can be processed using the MATLAB package, employing sophisticated state-space filtering methods. No new theory is presented, but to aid the reader the MATLAB code is provided which can be used for any application, as well as to illustrate the example shown, in a manner amenable to most practicing engineers. The example is based upon an aircraft engine, and shows data collected from flight and the linear system upon which the filter characteristics depend.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Sensitivity minimization with closed loop eigenvalues assignment
abstract: Develops a new procedure to minimize the L/sub 2/-norm of trajectory sensitivity functions alpha (t) and system input u(t) with prescribed closed-loop eigenvalues. Considering a linear time invariant system with multi-input, the parameter vectors in the state feedback matrix, proposed by Roppenecker for eigenvalues set, are used to derive necessary optimal conditions. An algorithm to achieve the minimal conditions is proposed. The advantages of the procedure is illustrated by one numerical example.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Homuncular learning and rule parallelism: an application to BACON
abstract: In complex knowledge systems control knowledge comprising condition-action rules is organised into knowledge sources or system operators. The paper presents a method for organising condition-action rules into a hierarchy of autonomous agents or homunculi in accordance with the tasks to be performed. In this architecture, actions are performed by action rules, tasks by homunculi and jobs by higher level homunculi. A system in this organisation can be trained at each homuncular level by explanation-based generalisation or by nonlinear classification. The paper first introduces a formalism for organising prescriptive knowledge into a homuncular hierarchy and defines homuncular learning and rule parallelism. It then describes how this method has been applied to transform the quantitative discovery program (BACON) due to P. Langley et al. (1987), into a hierarchic homuncular system and how it is trained to perform its tasks.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Application of the combined method of adaptive control to an aircraft control system
abstract: Advances in adaptive control theory have been reviving its application to the aircraft control problem. A combination of direct and indirect methods of adaptive control is applied to the pitch rate control system problem in the paper. The scheme used employs integral form adaptive laws. The paper presents the mathematics of the scheme; simulation results (using SIMNON package) for different flight conditions. The scheme offers the advantages of the combined method of adaptive control.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Multi-level signals with good autocorrelation properties
abstract: Considers a number of different types of multi-level (non-binary) signals with pseudorandom (PR) properties, ie impulsive (or near-impulsive) autocorrelation functions. Periodic and non-periodic types are discussed, as well as the synthesis of uncorrelated sets of multi level PR signals. The classes of signal described are multi-level m-signals, generalised Barker and other related complex signals, Huffman signal and non-binary complementary signal sets. Synthesis methods for each type are indicated.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An enhanced ultrasonic system for robot end effector tracking
abstract: There is widespread interest in the development of improved robot manipulator controllers, especially in the area of controlling the oscillatory modes associated with high speed manipulators. The common aim of such controllers is to steer the motion of the robot arm such that the end-effector adheres closely to some pre-specified trajectory. In order to verify the performance of any new controller when implemented on a real robot, the motion of the end-effector must be measured in real time. The use of end-effector position as an input parameter to the controller is also highly desirable. The typically fast movement of the end-effector imposes a requirement that the data rate of any end-effector position measurement system to be high. At a typical end-effector tip velocity of 1m/s, the end-effector moves 10 mm between samples if the data rate is 100 Hz. The solution proposed in the paper is the use of an ultrasonic position measurement and tracking system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An auto-tuning controller with supervised learning using neural nets
abstract: Concerns the use of neural nets in the feedback control of systems described by ordinary differential or difference equations. The controller is assumed to be of fixed structure but with free parameters that must be tuned to meet some previously chosen performance specifications. The supervisor consists of a neural net producing the actions and evaluating the success of failure of the selected action. An action is a point in the parameter space that is used to adjust a controller of fixed structure. Supervised learning is accomplished using a performance evaluator which alters conveniently the action network following a connectionist strategy. The analysis is based on the stochastic learning automaton, which selects an action according to a probability distribution that depends on the reinforcement signal produced by the performance evaluator. The feedback is, therefore, provided in the form of an evaluation of the results on the environment. The probability density over the action space is stored internally in the neural net, and the changes are incorporated by adjusting the synaptic weights in the learning phase.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Parameter bounds for linear models in the presence of bounded relative errors
abstract: Parameter bounding in linear static models with bounded relative output errors is outlined, based on equation-error and errors-invariables models. Two equation-error procedures are proposed, pointing out approximated and over evaluation of bounds on the equation error. It is shown that the problem can be reformulated in terms of errors-in-variables models and a method has been outlined, based on previous results of the author (1990). Orthotope outer-bounding approximations of the feasible parameter region, which allow the evaluation of parameter uncertainty intervals, have been considered. Both the over-bounded equation-error (OBEE) and the bounded errors-in-variables (BEIV) approach have been tested on simulated data, pointing out the superiority of BEIV to OBEE as far as parameter uncertainty intervals and computing time are concerned.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The electronic automation of weir gates on the River Thames
abstract: Presents a comprehensive design strategy for controlling the level of a river reach, using a distributed computer-based monitoring and control system that can be easily replicated. The river under investigation is the Thames and in particular the Caversham reach near Reading in Berkshire, in which a pilot plant has been successfully operated for two years.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Optimal PIP control of scalar and multivariable processes
abstract: At Sunderland Polytechnic, they have been using the object-oriented language SMALLTALK to help develop innovative solutions to new and old control problems. The paper is not about the expert system interface but is about an optimal proportional-integral-plus (PIP) control law design method which does appear to have some desirable features especially for those interested in installing real time digital, multivariable control systems, involving optimisation. All of the results presented were obtained using the advanced interface.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Concurrent processing in real-time simulation
abstract: The paper presents an assessment of the performance of transputers and Occam in the simulation of a third order nonlinear system. The primary objective of this study is to establish a framework for the development of a low-cost software-based real-time simulator for nonlinear multivariable systems. The choice of the electromagnetic suspension system as the 'demonstrator' is based mainly on its open-loop instability, its nonlinearity, and the detailed knowledge of the design requirements.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A bilinear self-tuning controller for industrial heating plant
abstract: Outlines preliminary simulation trials involving a novel self-tuning control strategy applied to a nonlinear model of an industrial heat treatment furnace. The nonlinear model is derived from physical considerations and takes into account the dominant radiative effects which are known to be prevalent in high temperature processes; the structure thus obtained is found to be bilinear. Open-loop tests on a high temperature box furnace have been carried out and time series analysis is used to validate the physical model. By accommodating the nonlinearity (bilinearity) into the self-tuning framework an extended pole-placement control strategy is proposed. To provide for a realistic comparison a measure of effectiveness is also proposed, which takes into account energy usage, maintenance and wear on actuators and penalty costs on large deviations from set-point. Results to date are encouraging and indicate that use of the bilinear self-tuning approach provides a potential improvement over existing state of the art controllers.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Task planning in an uncertain world
abstract: Given that so much is known about the issues involved in classical task planning and given the requirement for some form of predictive planning in a semi-autonomous or autonomous robot, the use of standard techniques is highly desirable. However, classical planners make strong and inappropriately restrictive assumptions about the world on which the planner operates which must be modified if a planner is to be usefully applied in robotic domains. The authors describe the work done in developing a prototype task planner called HELP (Hierarchical Execution-Led Planner) for such domains, and the way in which the classical approach has been adapted to cope with the relaxation of these assumptions.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An investigation into the use of nonlinear neural network architectures
abstract: Most research into neural nets has concentrated on either applications or learning algorithms. Comparatively little work has been done on studying the functional limitations imposed by the choice of network architecture. In this paper an investigation into the use of activation functions within the units of a network is presented. It is shown how such functions can affect the network behaviour, and why these changes take place. Efforts are particularly concentrated on the unit activation functions since they are likely to have a major impact on network performance and also since very little work has been carried out in this area. The results of this study lend confidence to the idea that considering alternative architectures may be useful.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Microprocessor based crane load state monitoring system
abstract: The objective of the paper is to develop a microprocessor-based system to monitor the load state and insure the safety of a mobile telescopic crane. The conventional microprocessor-based systems use the searching technique (look-up tables) to read the allowed load from the memory. The drawback of such technique is that it requires a large amount of memory space which would increase the size of the hardware and searching time. The solution adopted in the proposed design consists of developing an equation relating the specific working configurations to the allowed load. This method reduces greatly the memory space, since the microprocessor computes the allowed load from the coefficients, proper to each configuration. This result was checked by implementing the designed system on a mobile telescopic crane, model 1040, manufactured by ENMTP-CPG Company at Ain-Smara, Algeria.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An adaptive controller for industrial manipulators
abstract: Presents the study and design of an adaptive control method for an industrial manipulator. This method first presents an autoregressive time series model for the motion of the joints of a manipulator. The model parameters are obtained by using the data of the measured input-output pairs. Then, the estimated parameters of the manipulator are used to determine the controller gains on-line so that the desired path expressed at discrete points is followed as closely as possible. A feature of the authors' work is that it considers the inductance of armature circuit of the drive-motor, which is important for the stability of the control system. Finally, computer simulations are given to demonstrate to feasibility of the control scheme.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
